claim: Rapamycin increases lifespan in rodents.
source: The FDA approved drug rapamycin increases lifespan in rodents and delays age-related dysfunction in rodents and humans.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about rapamycin's effects.

claim: Rapamycin delays age-related dysfunction in rodents and humans.
source: The FDA approved drug rapamycin increases lifespan in rodents and delays age-related dysfunction in rodents and humans.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about rapamycin's effects.

claim: 3 months of rapamycin treatment is sufficient to increase life expectancy by up to 60% in middle-aged mice.
source: Here we show that 3 months of rapamycin treatment is sufficient to increase life expectancy by up to 60% and improve measures of healthspan in middle-aged mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by survival data in the results section.

claim: 3 months of rapamycin treatment improves measures of healthspan in middle-aged mice.
source: Here we show that 3 months of rapamycin treatment is sufficient to increase life expectancy by up to 60% and improve measures of healthspan in middle-aged mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by grip strength and rotarod data in the results section.

claim: Transient rapamycin treatment is associated with a remodeling of the microbiome.
source: This transient treatment is also associated with a remodeling of the microbiome, including dramatically increased prevalence of segmented filamentous bacteria in the small intestine.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data and histological analysis in the results section.

claim: Transient rapamycin treatment dramatically increases prevalence of segmented filamentous bacteria in the small intestine.
source: This transient treatment is also associated with a remodeling of the microbiome, including dramatically increased prevalence of segmented filamentous bacteria in the small intestine.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by real-time PCR, 16S rRNA sequencing, and histological data in the results section.

claim: A specific dose of rapamycin in female mice does not extend lifespan but is associated with a striking shift in cancer prevalence toward aggressive hematopoietic cancers and away from non-hematopoietic malignancies.
source: We also define a dose in female mice that does not extend lifespan, but is associated with a striking shift in cancer prevalence toward aggressive hematopoietic cancers and away from non-hematopoietic malignancies.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by histopathological analysis in the results section.

claim: A short-term rapamycin treatment late in life has persistent effects that can robustly delay aging.
source: These data suggest that a short-term rapamycin treatment late in life has persistent effects that can robustly delay aging, influence cancer prevalence, and modulate the microbiome.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: A short-term rapamycin treatment late in life influences cancer prevalence.
source: These data suggest that a short-term rapamycin treatment late in life has persistent effects that can robustly delay aging, influence cancer prevalence, and modulate the microbiome.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on histopathological findings.

claim: A short-term rapamycin treatment late in life modulates the microbiome.
source: These data suggest that a short-term rapamycin treatment late in life has persistent effects that can robustly delay aging, influence cancer prevalence, and modulate the microbiome.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on microbiome analysis.

claim: Successful interventions that increase healthy longevity in people could have profound benefits for quality of life, productivity, and reduced healthcare costs.
source: Successful interventions that increase healthy longevity in people could have profound benefits for quality of life, productivity, and reduced healthcare costs (Goldman et al., 2013; Kaeberlein et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Rapamycin has been shown to increase lifespan in numerous species.
source: The drug rapamycin is a promising candidate for such an intervention, as it has been shown to increase lifespan in numerous species (Johnson et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Rapamycin delays cognitive decline in mice.
source: it has been shown to increase lifespan in numerous species (Johnson et al., 2013) and to delay or reverse multiple age-associated phenotypes in mice including cognitive decline (Halloran et al., 2012; Majumder et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Rapamycin delays cardiac dysfunction in mice.
source: to delay or reverse multiple age-associated phenotypes in mice including cognitive decline (Halloran et al., 2012; Majumder et al., 2012), cardiac dysfunction (Dai et al., 2014; Flynn et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Rapamycin delays immune senescence in mice.
source: to delay or reverse multiple age-associated phenotypes in mice including cognitive decline (Halloran et al., 2012; Majumder et al., 2012), cardiac dysfunction (Dai et al., 2014; Flynn et al., 2013), immune senescence (Chen et al., 2009)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Rapamycin delays cancer in mice.
source: to delay or reverse multiple age-associated phenotypes in mice including cognitive decline (Halloran et al., 2012; Majumder et al., 2012), cardiac dysfunction (Dai et al., 2014; Flynn et al., 2013), immune senescence (Chen et al., 2009), and cancer (Anisimov et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: A six week treatment with the rapamycin derivative RAD001 was reported to improve immune function in elderly people, as measured by response to influenza vaccine.
source: Recently, a six week treatment with the rapamycin derivative RAD001 was reported to improve immune function in elderly people, as measured by response to influenza vaccine (Mannick et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: At least some of the effects of rapamycin on aging in mice are conserved in humans.
source: Recently, a six week treatment with the rapamycin derivative RAD001 was reported to improve immune function in elderly people, as measured by response to influenza vaccine (Mannick et al., 2014), suggesting that at least some of the effects on aging in mice are conserved in humans.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the introduction based on the RAD001 study.

claim: The utility of rapamycin or other mTOR inhibitors to delay aging may be limited by side effects.
source: Despite these impressive results, the utility of rapamycin or other mTOR inhibitors to delay aging may be limited by side effects.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a concern about rapamycin use.

claim: High doses of rapamycin and its derivatives used clinically to prevent organ transplant rejection are associated with adverse events, including impaired wound healing, edema, elevated circulating triglycerides, impaired glucose homeostasis, gastrointestinal discomfort, and mouth ulcers.
source: The high doses of rapamycin and its derivatives used clinically to prevent organ transplant rejection are associated with adverse events, including impaired wound healing, edema, elevated circulating triglycerides, impaired glucose homeostasis, gastrointestinal discomfort, and mouth ulcers (Augustine et al., 2007; de Oliveira et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Chronic treatment with encapsulated rapamycin (eRapa) in the diet at 14 ppm has been reported to cause gonadal degeneration in males, increased risk of cataracts, and impaired response to a glucose tolerance test.
source: While many of these side effects have not been observed in mice at the lower doses that extend lifespan, chronic treatment with encapsulated rapamycin (eRapa) in the diet at 14 ppm has been reported to cause gonadal degeneration in males, increased risk of cataracts, and impaired response to a glucose tolerance test (Wilkinson et al., 2012; Lamming et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The treatment regimen of 8 mg/kg rapamycin daily for 90 days was selected because it increases survival and alleviates disease phenotypes in short-lived mouse models of dilated cardiomyopathy, muscular dystrophy, and the severe mitochondrial disease Leigh Syndrome.
source: This dose was selected because we have previously found that it increases survival and alleviates disease phenotypes in short-lived mouse models of dilated cardiomyopathy, muscular dystrophy, and the severe mitochondrial disease Leigh Syndrome (Ramos et al., 2012; Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations.

claim: The 8 mg/kg/day injection treatment regimen is comparable to dietary delivery of eRapa at approximately 378 ppm.
source: Based on efficacy in the Leigh Syndrome mouse model and serum drug levels in wild type mice, we estimate that this treatment regimen is comparable to dietary delivery of eRapa at approximately 378 ppm (Johnson et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The 8 mg/kg/day injection treatment regimen is 27-fold higher levels than initially shown to extend lifespan in mice when continuous treatment is initiated at either 9 months or 20 months of age.
source: or 27-fold higher levels than initially shown to extend lifespan in mice when continuous treatment is initiated at either 9 months or 20 months of age (Harrison et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations.

claim: Prior studies have noted differences in the magnitude of lifespan extension following continuous rapamycin treatment in male versus female animals.
source: Because prior studies have noted differences in the magnitude of lifespan extension following continuous rapamycin treatment in male versus female animals (Harrison et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2011, 2014), we examined the effect of this regimen in both sexes independently.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations.

claim: Serum rapamycin levels did not differ significantly between male and female animals in the study.
source: Serum rapamycin levels did not differ significantly between male and female animals in our study (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: During the three-month treatment period, there was a significant decline in body weight of male mice receiving rapamycin injections relative to vehicle treated controls.
source: During the three-month treatment period, we noted a significant decline in body weight of male mice receiving rapamycin injections relative to vehicle treated controls (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Food intake remained similar during the treatment in male mice receiving rapamycin injections.
source: although food intake remained similar during the treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Decreased body weight persisted for several weeks following cessation of treatment in male mice receiving rapamycin injections.
source: Decreased body weight persisted for several weeks following cessation of treatment (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The 8 mg/kg/day rapamycin injection regimen resulted in a striking increase in median life expectancy from the end of treatment of 60% (p=0.02) in male mice.
source: This was accompanied by a striking increase in median life expectancy from the end of treatment of 60% (p=0.02, Figure 1B, Table 1)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by survival data shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: The 8 mg/kg/day rapamycin injection regimen resulted in an increase in overall median lifespan from birth of 16% (p=0.03) in male mice.
source: and an increase in overall median lifespan from birth of 16% (p=0.03, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by survival data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Table 2.

claim: The effect of the 8 mg/kg/day rapamycin injection regimen on male lifespan is larger than both the absolute and relative magnitude of lifespan extension resulting from continuous treatment to death with 14 ppm eRapa starting at around the same age in UMHET3 mice.
source: This effect is larger than both the absolute and relative magnitude of lifespan extension resulting from continuous treatment to death with 14 ppm eRapa starting at around the same age in UMHET3 mice (Harrison et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison stated in the results section and supported by citation.

claim: The longest-lived rapamycin-treated male in the cohort survived for 710 days post treatment to approximately 1400 days of age.
source: The longest-lived rapamycin-treated male in our cohort survived for 710 days post treatment to approximately 1400 days of age.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation from the survival data.

claim: The longest-lived rapamycin-treated male is likely one of the longest-lived wild type C57BL/6 animals ever reported.
source: Based on a survey of the literature, this is likely one of the longest-lived wild type C57BL/6 animals ever reported.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on a literature survey.

claim: The 8 mg/kg/day rapamycin injection regimen resulted in a decline in body weight of female mice.
source: This rapamycin regimen also resulted in a decline in body weight of female mice together with an increased trend of food intake in vehicle-treated animals with time (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The 8 mg/kg/day rapamycin injection regimen failed to increase post-treatment survival and lifespan in females (p=0.261).
source: however, we failed to detect a similar increase in post-treatment survival and lifespan in females (p=0.261, Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Tables 1–2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by survival data shown in Figure 2B and Tables 1-2.

claim: Cox proportional hazards regression with robust standard errors and adjusting for cohort indicated significant evidence of a treatment difference between male and female mice (p=0.023).
source: Cox proportional hazards regression with robust standard errors and adjusting for cohort indicated significant evidence of a treatment difference between male and female mice (p=0.023).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a statistical analysis result.

claim: The lack of lifespan extension in females results from an increase in aggressive hematopoietic cancers in the rapamycin treated females.
source: We speculated that this lack of lifespan extension results from an increase in aggressive hematopoietic cancers in the rapamycin treated females.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the results section, later supported by histopathological data.

claim: All the rapamycin-treated females examined (16 out of 16) had round cell tumors.
source: Histopathological analysis showed that while 6/12 control females had round cell tumors (lymphoma and histiocytic sarcoma of hematopoietic origins), comparable to previous studies in C57BL/6 mice (Blackwell et al., 1995; Treuting et al., 2008), all the rapamycin-treated females examined (16 out of 16) had round cell tumors (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, p=0.002).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by histopathological data shown in Figure 3.

claim: 6/12 control females had round cell tumors (lymphoma and histiocytic sarcoma of hematopoietic origins).
source: Histopathological analysis showed that while 6/12 control females had round cell tumors (lymphoma and histiocytic sarcoma of hematopoietic origins), comparable to previous studies in C57BL/6 mice (Blackwell et al., 1995; Treuting et al., 2008)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by histopathological data.

claim: An uncommon variant of lymphoma with plasmacytoid morphology affected 4 out of 16 mice examined in the rapamycin group and no vehicle treated mice.
source: Additionally, an uncommon variant of lymphoma with plasmacytoid morphology affected 4 out of 16 mice examined in the rapamycin group and no vehicle treated mice (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by histopathological data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Round cell tumors affected more organs in rapamycin treated females, with multiple (≥2) organs affected in all of the rapamycin treated females compared to only 3 vehicle treated females (p=0.01).
source: Round cell tumors affected more organs in rapamycin treated females, with multiple (≥2) organs affected in all of the rapamycin treated females compared to only 3 vehicle treated females (Figure 3C, p=0.01).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by histopathological data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The data indicate a more aggressive phenotype of hematopoietic tumors in the high dose rapamycin treated females.
source: Together, these data indicate a more aggressive phenotype of hematopoietic tumors in the high dose rapamycin treated females.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on histopathological findings.

claim: The incidence of non-hematopoietic neoplasms was dramatically decreased in the rapamycin group of females.
source: In contrast, the incidence of non-hematopoietic neoplasms was dramatically decreased in the rapamycin group (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by histopathological data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Nine non-hematopoietic neoplasms (5 pituitary adenomas, and 2 pulmonary adenomas, and 2 thyroid adenomas) were detected in 7 out of the 12 examined vehicle treated female mice.
source: Nine non-hematopoietic neoplasms (5 pituitary adenomas, and 2 pulmonary adenomas, and 2 thyroid adenomas) were detected in 7 out of the 12 examined vehicle treated mice
evidence: This is stated in the results section as histopathological findings.

claim: Only 1 out of 16 rapamycin treated females had non-hematopoietic neoplasia (1 pituitary adenoma) (p=0.004).
source: whereas, only 1 out of 16 rapamycin treated females had non-hematopoietic neoplasia (1 pituitary adenoma) (Figure 3D, p=0.004).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by histopathological data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: This regimen of rapamycin treatment induced the detrimental side effect of aggressive hematopoietic cancers specifically in female mice.
source: Although the number of mice examined is relatively small, based on these observations we speculate that this regimen of rapamycin treatment induced the detrimental side effect of aggressive hematopoietic cancers specifically in female mice
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the results section based on histopathological findings.

claim: Aggressive hematopoietic cancers in rapamycin-treated females occurred earlier in life and were sufficient to prevent lifespan extension despite other beneficial effects, such as reduced non-hematopoietic cancers.
source: which occurred earlier in life and were sufficient to prevent lifespan extension in these animals despite other beneficial effects, such as reduced non-hematopoietic cancers.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the results section based on survival and histopathological data.

claim: When data from both sexes are pooled together, daily injection of 8 mg/kg rapamycin for three months resulted in a non-significant (p=0.16) increase in life expectancy of 23%.
source: When data from both sexes are pooled together, daily injection of 8 mg/kg rapamycin for three months resulted in a non-significant (p=0.16) increase in life expectancy of 23% (Table 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Table 3.

claim: Between randomization and the end of treatment, 5 male mice (3 vehicle, 2 rapamycin) died of non-age related causes and were excluded from the analysis.
source: Between randomization and the end of treatment, 5 male mice (3 vehicle, 2 rapamycin) died of non-age related causes and were excluded from the analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a methodological detail.

claim: Inclusion of the 5 male mice that died of non-age related causes in the analysis of survival does not significantly affect the results.
source: Their inclusion in the analysis of survival does not significantly affect the results as described above (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Body weight and food intake were largely unaffected by the 126 ppm eRapa dietary regimen.
source: In contrast with the effects of daily injection of 8 mg/kg rapamycin (Figures 1A and 2A), body weight and food intake were largely unaffected by this dietary rapamycin regimen (Figure 4 A,C,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: There was a transient, small increase in body weight in female mice fed eRapa.
source: except for a transient, small increase in body weight in female mice fed eRapa, as determined by Student's t test (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Median post-treatment life expectancy was significantly increased by 42% when female and male animals were considered together (p=0.002) with the 126 ppm eRapa dietary regimen.
source: Median post-treatment life expectancy was significantly increased by 42% when female and male animals were considered together (p=0.002, Figure 4B, Table 3)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by survival data shown in Figure 4B and Table 3.

claim: Overall lifespan was increased by 13% (p=0.003) with the 126 ppm eRapa dietary regimen.
source: and overall lifespan was increased by 13% (p=0.003, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, Table 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by survival data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and Table 4.

claim: Three months of 126 ppm eRapa administration significantly increased post-treatment survival in both males and females independently.
source: Similar results were observed stratifying on sex; three months of 126 ppm eRapa administration significantly increased post-treatment survival in both males and females independently (Figure 4D,F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C and Tables 1–2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by survival data shown in Figure 4 and Tables 1-2.

claim: Cox proportional hazards regression with robust standard error estimates did not find evidence that sex modifies the treatment effect of 126 ppm eRapa (p=0.904).
source: Cox proportional hazards regression with robust standard error estimates did not find evidence that sex modifies the treatment effect (p=0.904).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a statistical analysis result.

claim: Between randomization and the end of treatment, 1 male mouse died of non-age related causes and was excluded from the analysis.
source: Between randomization and the end of treatment, 1 male mouse died of non-age related causes and was excluded from the analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a methodological detail.

claim: Inclusion of the 1 male mouse that died of non-age related causes in the analysis does not significantly affect the results.
source: Its inclusion in the analysis does not significantly affect the results as described above (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Eudragit-fed mice showed a steady decline in both grip strength and Rotarod performance.
source: While eudragit-fed mice showed a steady decline in both grip strength and Rotarod performance, rapamycin-fed mice scored significantly better than control mice in both assays after treatment (Figure 4G,H)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4G,H.

claim: Rapamycin-fed mice scored significantly better than control mice in both grip strength and Rotarod assays after treatment.
source: While eudragit-fed mice showed a steady decline in both grip strength and Rotarod performance, rapamycin-fed mice scored significantly better than control mice in both assays after treatment (Figure 4G,H)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4G,H.

claim: The healthspan promoting effect of rapamycin continues after treatment is discontinued.
source: rapamycin-fed mice scored significantly better than control mice in both assays after treatment (Figure 4G,H), suggesting that the healthspan promoting effect of rapamycin continues after treatment is discontinued.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the grip strength and rotarod data.

claim: Only rapamycin-fed mice showed a progressive increase in Rotarod performance during the 3 days of training and over the whole study, with mice performing better at 6 months compared to baseline.
source: Furthermore, only rapamycin-fed mice showed a progressive increase in Rotarod performance during the 3 days of training and over the whole study, with mice performing better at 6 months compared to baseline (Figure 4H, large bracket).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Mice treated with either rapamycin regimen produced consistently smaller fecal pellets than age-matched controls.
source: In the course of routine animal husbandry, we noted that mice treated with either rapamycin regimen produced consistently smaller fecal pellets than age-matched controls (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The difference in feces size was present in both dry and freshly excreted feces.
source: This difference was present in both dry (Figure 5C,D) and freshly excreted feces (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Water content is not a major factor affecting feces size in rapamycin-treated mice.
source: This difference was present in both dry (Figure 5C,D) and freshly excreted feces (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), indicating that water content is not a major factor affecting feces size.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the feces weight data.

claim: Feces size was affected independently of the method of rapamycin delivery.
source: In addition, feces size was affected independently of the method of rapamycin delivery (Figure 5C,D)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The effect of rapamycin on feces size was persistent after cessation of treatment.
source: and the effect was persistent after cessation of treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Changes in the microbiome may underlie the feces size phenotype in rapamycin-treated mice.
source: We hypothesized that changes in the microbiome may underlie this phenotype and therefore analyzed the fecal microbiome for each of the cohorts used in this study by deep-sequencing of bacterial 16S rRNA.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the results section.

claim: Rapamycin treatment induced a significant change in the composition of fecal microbiome (p=0.018 for injection cohorts, p=0.015 for feeding cohorts, p=0.005 for pooled cohorts).
source: Distance based permutation multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) (Anderson, 2001) indicated that rapamycin treatment induced a significant change in the composition of fecal microbiome (p=0.018 for injection cohorts. p=0.015 for feeding cohorts.p=0.005 for pooled cohorts), even after accounting for delivery method and batch effects (Figure 6—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by microbiome analysis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: Among the most notable changes in fecal bacterial DNA content was a significant increase in prevalence of segmented filamentous bacteria (SFB, Candidatus Arthromitus sp.) in the rapamycin treated animals.
source: Among the most notable changes in fecal bacterial DNA content seen in the global microbiome analysis was a significant increase in prevalence of segmented filamentous bacteria (SFB, Candidatus Arthromitus sp.) in the rapamycin treated animals (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by microbiome analysis data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: SFB are intestinal Gram-positive bacteria with a segmented and filamentous morphology.
source: SFB are intestinal Gram-positive bacteria with a segmented and filamentous morphology, and are not normally present at high levels in aged mice (Ericsson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation.

claim: SFB are not normally present at high levels in aged mice.
source: SFB are intestinal Gram-positive bacteria with a segmented and filamentous morphology, and are not normally present at high levels in aged mice (Ericsson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The SFB genome lacks a majority of virulence factors and SFB are not invasive.
source: The SFB genome lacks a majority of virulence factors and SFB are not invasive (Prakash et al., 2011)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation.

claim: SFB's tight adhesion to the intestinal epithelial cell induces differentiation of host immune cells.
source: however, their tight adhesion to the intestinal epithelial cell induces differentiation of host immune cells (Atarashi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The increase in SFB following rapamycin treatment was confirmed by real-time PCR of DNA from fecal samples obtained from both mice receiving injections or encapsulated rapamycin.
source: The increase in SFB following rapamycin treatment was confirmed by real-time PCR of DNA from fecal samples obtained from both mice receiving injections or encapsulated rapamycin (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The increase in SFB following rapamycin treatment was confirmed by semi-quantitative histological scoring of the small intestine in an independent cohort of mice.
source: as well as by semi-quantitative histological scoring of the small intestine in an independent cohort of mice obtained from the Harrison Lab at the Jackson Laboratory and injected with 8 mg/kg/day of for 3 months at the University of Washington (Figure 6C,D, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by histological data shown in Figure 6C,D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Increased SFB DNA was observed both in mice injected with rapamycin and mice fed dietary eRapa, indicating this effect is independent of mode of drug delivery.
source: Since increased SFB DNA was observed both in mice injected with rapamycin and mice fed dietary eRapa, this effect is independent of mode of drug delivery.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the SFB data.

claim: This represents the first pharmacological intervention to increase SFB in any animal.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first pharmacological intervention to increase SFB in any animal.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a claim about the novelty of the finding.

claim: A single three-month regimen of rapamycin is sufficient to robustly increase life expectancy in middle-aged mice, comparable to the effects previously reported for life-long treatment.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrate that a single three-month regimen of rapamycin is sufficient to robustly increase life expectancy in middle-aged mice, comparable to the effects previously reported for life-long treatment
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: A single three-month regimen of rapamycin improves measures of healthspan in middle-aged mice.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrate that a single three-month regimen of rapamycin is sufficient to robustly increase life expectancy in middle-aged mice, comparable to the effects previously reported for life-long treatment, while also improving measures of healthspan
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: A single three-month regimen of rapamycin substantially alters the microbiome.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrate that a single three-month regimen of rapamycin is sufficient to robustly increase life expectancy in middle-aged mice, comparable to the effects previously reported for life-long treatment, while also improving measures of healthspan and substantially altering the microbiome.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: This work extends prior evidence indicating that short-term rapamycin treatment can improve health in mice.
source: This work extends prior evidence indicating that short-term rapamycin treatment can improve health in mice, including one experiment suggesting that 4 mg/kg rapamycin every other day for 6 weeks enhanced survival until around 30 months of age in a small cohort (Chen et al., 2009)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: 4 mg/kg rapamycin every other day for 6 weeks enhanced survival until around 30 months of age in a small cohort.
source: including one experiment suggesting that 4 mg/kg rapamycin every other day for 6 weeks enhanced survival until around 30 months of age in a small cohort (Chen et al., 2009)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation.

claim: Studies have reported improvements in cardiac function following transient treatment with rapamycin.
source: and studies reporting improvements in cardiac (Dai et al., 2014; Flynn et al., 2013) and immune (Chen et al., 2009) function following transient treatment with rapamycin.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Studies have reported improvements in immune function following transient treatment with rapamycin.
source: and studies reporting improvements in cardiac (Dai et al., 2014; Flynn et al., 2013) and immune (Chen et al., 2009) function following transient treatment with rapamycin.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: In the animals treated with the 126 ppm eRapa diet, the improvements in lifespan and health were achieved without overt detrimental side effects.
source: In the animals treated with the 126 ppm eRapa diet in this study, the improvements in lifespan and health were achieved without overt detrimental side effects, although it is possible that some side effects were undetected, and we did not explicitly test for cataracts, gonadal degeneration, and other adverse outcomes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an observation from the study.

claim: In the case of the 8 mg/kg/day injection regimen, serious side effects were noted in female, but not male mice.
source: In the case of the 8 mg/kg/day injection regimen, serious side effects were noted in female, but not male mice.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an observation from the study.

claim: A dramatic shift toward aggressive hematopoietic cancers and away from non-hematopoietic cancers was observed in female mice treated with 8 mg/kg/day rapamycin injections.
source: Intriguingly, a dramatic shift toward aggressive hematopoietic cancers and away from non-hematopoietic cancers was observed in these female mice.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an observation from the study.

claim: The shift toward aggressive hematopoietic cancers in rapamycin-treated female mice is consistent with a similar weak trend seen in kidney transplant patients receiving rapamycin to prevent organ rejection.
source: This is consistent with a similar weak trend seen in kidney transplant patients receiving rapamycin to prevent organ rejection, suggesting a possible conservation of mechanism and clinical relevance (Mathew et al., 2004).
